summary: Describes how to map ISUP overlap signalling to SIP. This is needed when a SIP call involves interworking with the public telephone network. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Old phone systems accept a number a few digits at a time. This memo says how to translate that digit-by-digit way of dialing into an internet call setup.

questions: how does a sip gateway handle overlap dialing
what are t10 and t35 timers in isup to sip
subtitle: How a gateway turns digit-by-digit PSTN dialing into SIP calls, and when it is safe to pass the digits on as they arrive.

tldr.problem: Some parts of the telephone network send a called number a few digits at a time (overlap signalling), but SIP always carries the whole address in the INVITE.
tldr.mechanism: The preferred approach is for the gateway to collect digits using number analysis and timers, then send one INVITE. Where that delay is unacceptable, the gateway may send several INVITEs with growing digit strings, but only under strict routing conditions.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives procedures in both directions and warns that overlap in SIP is only safe when INVITEs reach a single gateway and no valid number is a prefix of another.

today: RFC 3578 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the en-bloc mapping in RFC 3398.

sections.title: En-bloc and Overlap Signalling
sections.content:
RFC 3398 maps SIP to the ISDN User Part (ISUP) of SS7, but only for en-bloc signalling, where the complete callee number is in the first message. Overlap signalling sends only some digits first and the rest in later messages. Modern switches always use en-bloc, but some parts of the PSTN still use overlap, and the RFC says it is still in use in some countries.

SIP is en-bloc: the Request-URI of an INVITE always contains the whole callee address. The preferred solution is therefore to convert overlap into en-bloc SIP using number analysis and timers (Section 2 of the RFC). Because that can cause unacceptable multi-second setup delays for human users, Section 3 analyzes using overlap signalling inside the SIP network and where it is acceptable.
sections.eli5: Old phone lines hand over a number in pieces. Internet calls want the whole number first, so something has to either wait for all the pieces or pass them on carefully.

sections.title: Converting Overlap to En-bloc
sections.content:
The gateway first receives an IAM (Initial Address Message) holding part of the number. The remaining digits arrive in one or more SAMs (Subsequent Address Messages).

If the IAM holds fewer digits than the minimum needed to route a call, the gateway starts timer T35 and waits for the minimum number of digits or a stop digit. If T35 expires first, it sends a REL with cause value 28 to the ISUP side. Q.764 defines T35 as 15-20 seconds. A stop digit lets the gateway send the INVITE at once.

Once the minimum is reached, the gateway uses number analysis to decide whether the number is complete. If it cannot tell, it collects digits until timer T10 expires or a stop digit (the RFC gives the hash character as its example) arrives. T10 is refreshed on every new digit. When it expires, an INVITE with the digits so far is sent and any later SAM is ignored.

Q.764 recommends a T10 range of 4-6 seconds; the RFC recommends that range, but the actual value is a matter of local policy.
sections.eli5: The gateway listens to the digits and keeps a stopwatch that restarts with each one. When no more digits arrive in time, it places the call with the number it has.

sections.title: One INVITE or Several
sections.content:
One idea for sending overlap into SIP is to send an INVITE with the IAM digits and then pass SAM digits in a request such as INFO inside the early dialog. The RFC does not recommend this. It needs the far side to send a non-100 provisional response at once, which gateways following RFC 3398 do not do. Making them do so (for example with a 183 Session Progress) would cause early ACMs and confuse the PSTN state machine. Also, all later requests follow the first path and cannot be rerouted to use SIP services.

The alternative is a new INVITE with all digits so far every time a SAM arrives. Each is a new transaction and can be routed differently, which is a benefit and a problem: two INVITEs may reach two gateways, each generating an IAM, and an incomplete number would fail after using PSTN resources.

So a gateway can be configured to generate SIP overlap only if the SIP routing infrastructure ensures INVITEs reach just one gateway. If the infrastructure is not under the administrator's control, the Section 2 procedures must be used. SIP overlap also should not be used toward parts of the PSTN where a number and a shorter prefix of it can both be valid addresses of different terminals.
sections.eli5: Sending a fresh note each time a new digit arrives is fast, but the notes might go to different offices. It is only safe if every note is sure to reach the same one.

sections.title: Generating Multiple INVITEs
sections.content:
As soon as the minimum number of digits is received, the gateway sends an INVITE built as in RFC 3398 and starts T10. When a SAM arrives, T10 is refreshed and a new INVITE goes out. It has the same Call-ID and the same From header field (including the tag) as the first, an updated Request-URI with all digits so far, and a To header with all digits but no tag.

The new INVITE should not use the To tag or a Route header from any response to the earlier INVITE, so the network can route it dynamically. Its CSeq is recommended to be higher than any CSeq the gateway has used for that Call-ID, to avoid confusion with early dialogs created by forking.

If the gateway encapsulates ISUP messages as SIP bodies, it should include the IAM and all SAMs received so far.
sections.eli5: Each new note repeats everything dialed so far and carries the same call label, but it does not reuse any reply stamp from earlier notes.

sections.title: Responses, REL and CANCEL
sections.content:
If 4xx, 5xx or 6xx final responses (for example 484 Address Incomplete) arrive before T10 expires, the gateway should not send any REL. It sends one only when no more SAMs arrive, T10 expires and every INVITE has had a final response other than 200 OK. The REL cause value comes from the best response among all INVITEs, computed as a forking proxy would, as in RFC 3398. The best response is not always the one to the INVITE with most digits: a mistaken extra digit could give a 486 (Busy Here) for the first and a 484 for the second.

All responses except typically one are 400 class responses. A 183 Session Progress with media may also arrive; as a general rule, the media stream from the INVITE with more digits has priority.

A gateway should not CANCEL the previous INVITE when it sends a new one, since the CANCEL could reach the egress gateway first and trigger a REL. Once a 200 OK arrives, it should CANCEL all the other INVITE transactions, and it may wait a while first so they can finish without extra signalling.
sections.eli5: The gateway hangs up on the caller only when everyone has said no and no more digits are coming. If someone says yes, it politely cancels all the other tries.

sections.title: SIP to ISUP Direction
sections.content:
When the call starts in the SIP network, the gateway may receive several INVITEs with the same Call-ID but different Request-URIs. The first INVITE produces an IAM as in RFC 3398.

A later INVITE with the same Call-ID and From tag and an updated Request-URI should produce a SAM instead of a new IAM, and the earlier INVITE is answered with 484 Address Incomplete. If the gateway is attached to a PSTN area that uses en-bloc signalling, it should instead generate a REL for the previous IAM and a new IAM.
sections.eli5: When the internet side keeps sending longer numbers, the gateway adds the new digits to the same phone call, unless the phone side cannot take digits in pieces, in which case it starts over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With overlap signalling, an attacker could send multiple INVITEs with an incomplete address to the same gateway to occupy all available ports and deny service. Since none of these calls would complete, the sender might never be billed under a traditional scheme.

The authors recommend that gateway operators authenticate INVITE senders, for accountability and so the gateway can see many calls from one source in a short time. The gateway should track a threshold of hanging overlap calls and reject further similar calls once it is exceeded.
sections.eli5: Someone could start lots of half-dialed calls to use up all the phone lines. The gateway should know who is calling and stop taking more once too many are left hanging.
